opus-5.5.text:
Well, I find that hypothesis really compelling, though I hold it with some humility, because it's still very much an open question in cognitive science.

The idea, which comes from people like George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, Lawrence Barsalou, and others in the embodied cognition tradition, is that even our most abstract concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. We understand time in terms of space: the future is "ahead of us," the past is "behind us." We talk about ideas being "grasped," arguments being "built" or "falling apart," people being "close" to us emotionally. Lakoff and Johnson argued these aren't just figures of speech; they reflect how we actually think. Our abstract reasoning seems to be scaffolded on metaphors drawn from having a body that moves through a physical world.

There's some interesting experimental evidence for this too. Studies show that physical warmth can influence judgments of social warmth, or that thinking about the future versus the past can subtly shift people's posture forward or backward. Some of those results haven't replicated well, so I'm cautious about leaning on any single study, but the overall picture is suggestive.

What really interests me is what this means for AI. If human concepts bottom out in embodied experience, then it raises a deep question about systems like large language models, which learn purely from text. They're learning the *outputs* of embodied minds, the language that humans produced, without the underlying grounding. So they can manipulate the word "heavy" very fluently, but do they have anything like a concept of heaviness? I'm skeptical that they understand concepts the way we do. That shows up in their brittleness, in how they can fail in strange ways on problems that require genuine abstraction or transfer to novel situations.

That said, I don't want to be dogmatic. It's possible that some degree of conceptual structure can be extracted from language alone, since language carries an enormous amount of information about the world. The question is how far that gets you. My intuition is that robust, flexible understanding, the kind that lets you form analogies and apply concepts in genuinely new contexts, probably does require something like grounding, whether that's physical embodiment or at least rich interaction with an environment.

So I'd say I'm sympathetic to the hypothesis, I think it has profound implications for how we build AI, and I think we need much better science, both in understanding human cognition and in probing what our machines actually understand, before we can say anything definitive.

fable-5.1.text:
I find it very compelling, actually, though I'd put it a bit more carefully than "all our concepts bottom out in physical experience." The version I'm drawn to comes out of the work of people like Lakoff and Johnson, and also Lawrence Barsalou's work on grounded cognition. The idea is that even our most abstract concepts are built up through metaphor from a core of concepts that are grounded in our bodies and in how we move through and interact with the world.

So you take something like "understanding." We say we "grasp" an idea, we "get" something, an argument "goes over our heads." Or time: we talk about the future being ahead of us, about events coming up, about a deadline approaching. These aren't just decorative figures of speech. There's a lot of evidence from psychology and neuroscience that when people process these concepts, the same sensorimotor systems that are involved in actual grasping or actual spatial movement get recruited. That suggests the metaphors are doing real cognitive work, that abstract thought is in some sense simulated on top of the machinery we evolved for perceiving and acting.

Now, I'd stop short of saying that's the whole story. Culture and language clearly contribute a huge amount, and there's a lot of social scaffolding involved in how children acquire concepts. And "bottom out" is a strong phrase. I don't think anyone has shown that you can reductively trace every concept back to a specific set of bodily primitives. It's more that embodiment provides the foundation and the constraints, and then a lot gets built on top through analogy and through interaction with other people.

But where this really matters for me is in thinking about AI. If this view is even roughly right, then it raises a real question about systems that learn purely from text. Large language models are learning the statistical shadows of our concepts, the way we talk about things, without ever having had the experiences that, on this view, gave rise to those concepts in the first place. They've never grasped anything, never been in a space, never felt time pass. So one open question is whether you can really get the concepts themselves out of language alone, or whether you end up with something that looks a lot like understanding from the outside but is missing the grounding that makes human concepts robust and flexible. I honestly don't think we know the answer yet, but I think that's one of the most important questions in the field right now.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very compelling hypothesis, but I don’t think we know that it’s true. The idea is that even our very abstract concepts are grounded in our experience of having bodies and interacting with the world. We talk about understanding something as “grasping” it, or about a relationship as a journey. And those aren’t necessarily just figures of speech; they might reflect how we actually organize those concepts.

But there’s a gap between showing that physical experience shapes our thinking and showing that all concepts ultimately reduce to it. Mathematics is an interesting example. We can see how counting might arise from interacting with objects, but explaining how that gets you to very abstract mathematics is a much bigger task. So I take grounding seriously, but I think the question of how you build those layers of abstraction is still very much open.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something very compelling about that idea. Even when we talk about abstract things, we use language that comes from physical experience. We talk about grasping an idea, or being close to someone emotionally, or getting over a problem. That suggests that our understanding of abstract concepts is connected to the ways we perceive and act in the world.

But I’d distinguish that from saying we know that every concept ultimately bottoms out in physical experience. That’s a much stronger claim. We also learn through language, through other people, and through culture. The interesting question is how those different sources of understanding fit together, and what kinds of grounding an AI system would need to develop concepts that are robust and meaningful.
